DEPARTMENT OF STATE
DIVISION OF FAR EASTERN AFFAIRS
September 4, 1942
Tokyo's despatch of June 3, 1942, encloses
83 pages of "Notes on Eccnomic and Financial
Developments by the Commercial Attaché during
the period from December 8, 1941 to June 1, 1942
DCA has drafted an instruction to
Mr. Williams giving the report a rating of
excellent.
There are a number of subjects dealt with
in this report whioh are of interest to FE.
There are also a considerable number of sub-
jeots in the report which are not of interest
to FE. I have routed the despatoh to return
to FE and when it comes back I will prepare
separate memoranda on those subjects of inter-
est. This report should have come to the Depart
ment in the form of a number of despatches on
separate subjeots. By writing the proposed memo-
randa it will be possible to have the material
filed under the appropriate headings.
There are no extra copies of the report
as the extra copies have already been distri-
buted.

Enclosure No. 1 to Despatch dated June
3, 1942 from the Embassy at Tokyo.
ECONOMIC AND FINANCIAL NOTES COMPILED
FROM DECEMBER 8, 1 9 4 1
DEFENSE APPROPRIATIONS:
During 194l one ordinary (76tn) session and
two (77th and 78th) extraordinary sessions of the
Imperial Diet were held and budgetary appropriations
of these three bodis for lefense purposes reacned
Yen 1l,770 million. Tris figure urings the total war
appropriations since the outbreak of the China Incident
in July, 1937, to Yen 2, 009 million. The General
Accounts budget for the next fiscal year has been set
at Yen 6,210 million.
TAXES:
Indirect taxes were increased by a bill
approved by the 77th session of tne Diet to the extent
of an estimated Yen 630 million per annum. From
December 1, 1941 to arch 31, 1942 an additional
revenue of Yen 170 million is anticipated from this
source for this current fiscal year. The 79tn session
of the Diet is expected to adopt a plan for a broad
expansion in direct taxes to be enforced during the
1942-43 fiscal year.
BOND ISSUES:
Mr. T. Yuki, Governor of the Bank of Japan,
reportedly announced on December 24th that the Government
had released Yen 6,500 million worth of national bonds
from January 1 to December 15, 194l. This figure is
higher by Yen 2,720 million than that for the corres-
ponding period of 1940. The Governor also announced
that

WHOLESALE PRICE:
The Ministry of Comaerce & Industry's whole-
sale price index for tne nation for November rose to
181.8 (1929 = 100), ga1ns of 0.5 over October, 8.9
over November, 1940 and 49.3% over June, 1937. Against
October prices merchandise, foodstuffs and fiber goods
were higher by 1%, metal articles by 0.6%, building
materials by O.2% and fuel by O.1%. Sundries fell

STRENGTHENED FINA.CIAL CO..TROL
Two oxtremely important ordinances, designed
to strengthen the Government's control over wartime
economy, were approved on tne 19th of January. Both
were formulated in accordance with the National Mobiliza-
tion Law. The first, the Financial Urganizations
Control Ordinance, inaugurates a dual control system.
It provides for the establishment of various control
associations for major banks, local banks, trust firms,
life insurance underwriters and other financial institu-
tions, and in addition the creation of a National
Financing Control Association which will have supreme
authority over these several control bodies. The
governor of the Bank of Japan will head this Assoclation
and

the shapine of the nntional nonetary policies.

among banks; (5) the furtnerance of the liaison be-

The second ordinance, the Ordinance Relating

designed to accelerate the amalgamation of banks,

FOUR POINT POLICY FOR CO-PROSPERITY SPHERE AS
ANNOUNCED IN DIET O. JANUARY 23. 1942
The premier on January 23, 1.42 clarified
the Government's policy for the adminisiration of
occupied areas. This policy embraces the followin
measures:-
1. The acquirement of essential resources.
2. The prevention of vital materials found in
the southern regions from finding their way
into enemy countries.
3. Insuring the self-support of Japanese forces
in the areas in which they are operating.
4. Inducing established concerns in occupied
territories to cooperate with Japan.

BATIONING OF CLOTHES
Effective February 1, 1942 tne Japanese
Government will place tne distribution of clotning
materials, clothes and t..eir accessories on a
tioket system. Eacn person will be allowed lo0
points per annum. The reasons  iven for this drastic
step include Japan's inability to purahase raw cotton
from abroad and the necessity of exporting silk, rayon
and staple fibre to countries in the East Asia Co-
prosperity Sphere. The number of wholesale dealers
in textiles is to be drastically curtailed and a central
cloth distributing concern organized for each of the
larger cities.
WHOLESALE PRICE - DECEMBER, 1941
The Ministry of Commerce and Industry's
wholesale price index for all of Japan for December
rose 1.1% over November to 183.8 (December 1929 - 100).
As compared with the corresponding month of 1940 the
gain was 9.3% and with June, 1937 the advance was
50.9%. Metal goods were higher by 2.1%, foodstuffs
by 1.5%, textiles by 1.1%, building materials by 0.7%
and fuel by 0.1% than during November, 1941. Mis-
cellaneous artioles deolined by 0.8% and chemicals by
0.5%. Fertilisers were unchanged.

THE BAHT-YEN EXCHANGE ACCORD
As a forward step in solidifying Jacan's domination
of all economic and financial policies and developments in
the Greater East Asia sphere, an accord was reached on
April 22nd linking the two currencies at par value. Since
January 1, 1942 the rate has been 100 bahts equals Yen 155.70
but this was only a temporary arrangement pendin: the
development of Japan's more extensive plan for complete
control of the monetary systems of all units of the new
sphere. This control entails: (1) the settlement in Tokyo
of all monetary transactions among the sphere countries;
(2) the conclusion by the Bank of Japan of foreign exchange
contracts with control banks which are to be set up in each
unit country, and (3) the installation of the Bank of Japan
as the central bank in entire co-prosperity sphere.
Prices of exchangeable commodities are not to

Tokyo, Nov. 3. The Great East Asia Ministry was
established for construoting the Great Bast Asia Co-
prosperity Circle. Ever since the Manchuria and China
incidents, the enterprise of constructing Great Bast
Asia has been carried on by Japan. Since the outbreak
of the Great East Asia War, Japan has succeeded in
occupying a large area in the South Seas in less than
a year. In order to attain political and economic
collaboration, the new Ministry has been inaugurated.
Hereafter, not only the ambassadors and ministers in
the Great East Asia area will be under the control of
the new Ministry, but also the Ministry of Colonies,
the Manchurian Affeirs Bureau and the South Seas Bureau
will be amalgamated to the new Ministry. The establish-
ment of the Ministry will go a long way in economic
construotion in Great East Asia. Work of economic con-
struetion in Great East Asia may be summarized as follows:
1. Manchuria: Since 1938 Japan and Manohuria has formed
one unit in pushing the 5-year plan, and special efforts
and attention have been devoted to iron and coal produo-
tion. Regarding agrioulture, a state of self-support and
self-suffioiency has been attained for Japan and Manchuria.
2. China: Since the establishment of the National Polioy
Co. in l939, China has come to a stage of long-period
construction. The enterprises and telegraphic communica-
tions are developing successfully. 3. South Seas: The
regions in the South Sees have ebundant resources such as
petroleum, rubbe, tin, iron, copper, wolfram, etc. The
possession of petroleum by Japan in these regions will be
holpful in carrying Japan successfully through the war.
Rubber, which is badly required by America, is also in
Japan's possession. The exploitation of these resourees
will not only have close bearing on our war operations
but will also bring emancipation to all the peoples in
the South Seas, so that they will enjoy where they are.
All plans made during wartime have bearing on the war.
The Great East Asia War is generally called a war of
sc'entifie construction. The Great East Asia Co-prosperity
Cirole, which was harmed by Britain and America, will by
virtue of the establishment of the new Ministry form a
link in the new world order

V. MANPOWER
Labor mobilization. The tightened Japanese manpower
situation has resulted in government decisions to expand
national registration of labor, to extend technical training.
and to establish a fundamental policy for housing and wage con-
trol. Civilian labor mobilization has been expanded to include
the whole population. The Imperial Rule Assistance Association
is taking a more active role in the utilization of the Japanese
for war work.
Impairment of labor force. Thero has been a considerable
increase in the accident rate due in part to long working hours
and consequent fatigue, a deterioration in the general health
of workers, the failure to provide adequate safety devices for
machines and, above all, to a rapid influx of young and inex-
perienced workers into industries. In December 1942 the length
of the working day in war plants was cut to 10 hours. .The rise
in the number of tubercular patients due to less food (parti-
cularly rice and vegetables), less fuel and poorer clothing is
reflected in a report that 80 percent of the budget of 133
milllon yen of the Welfare Ministry will be devoted to an. anti-
tuberoular campaign.

VI.ADMINISTRATION
Struggle for control of war production. An internal
struggle between the various groups which control Japan's
industry has been raging for years. The conflict power over
Japanese war production reached a high point during the past
two months. Most of the various Japanese industries have been
grouped into various control associations which in turn are
placed under the direction of various ministries. A plan
worked out two or three months ago whereby the President of
the army-dominated Planning Board was to be chairman of a
cabinet committee made up of the various departmental ministers
left too much control in the hands of the ministries.
The most recent move was disclosed in the announcement
of the provisions of two Imperial ordinances for which approvai
by the Diet was requested. One ordinance elevates Premier Tojo
above the other cabinet ministers, the other ordinance gives
him dictatorial powers enabling him to control war-time produo-
tion. The Premier, no doubt, will share from the operational
viewpoint his new powers with the army-dominated Planning Board.
This board which had been mainly an advisory group will now have
a great increase of power and influence in Japan's war-time
economy. Five so-called "nucleus" industries--aircraft, ship-
building, iron and steel, coal mining and the light metals--
have been given priority status. Operational authority is
being centered in the cabinet under Tojo's immediate direction.
Currency controls and inflation. In the administration
of the conquered areas, the Japanese have been utilizing currency
manipulations to further their controls. Agreements are being
made which adopt the Japanese yen in the settlement of all
trade balances. Local currencies will eventually be pesged to
the Japanese yen rather than to the military yen which has besn
used. In some areas, occupfed China particularly, imflationary
bendempies are still a basic problem.

Missionary Properties in Peiping Transferred:
Peiping, Dec. lOth. American and British churches
were taken over by the Chinese authorities in Peiping
on March 14, 1942. Now, the right of using and control-
ling the residences of all American and British
missionaries has also been transferred to China from
the special service organizations of Japan. At 3:00 p.m.
yesterday, a removal ceremony for American and British
missionaries was held and was participated by representa-
tives of Japanese special service organizations, American
and British missionaries and Chinese pastors.
3.
Communication and Intelligence Network in Malaya:
Singapore, Dec. l2th. Considerable progress has
been made in the communication and intelligence network
under the control of the military authorities in Malaya.
On September 29th, a postal administration and intel-
ligence office were established in Singapore. Lately,
a marine affairs office and a public utility office were
also established. Recently, it has been decided to
establish a broadcasting administration, a land survey
office, and a railway administration. An observatory
will also be operated by the military authorities to
facilitate ocean and air transport. General conditions
of these offices are as follows:
1. Intelligence office: head office in Singapore
with seven branches in various places in Malaya and
Sumatra. Telegraph and telephone offices are placed
under the control of these intelligence offices.
2. Postal administration: head office in Singapore
with eight postal administration offices in various
places in Malaya and Sumatra. These offices deal
principally in mails, parcels, postal remittances and
savings, and will in the future stárt business in life
insurance.
3. Marine affairs office: offices were established
in Singapore and Medan on October lst. Work is now being
devoted to junk building and registration of junks.
Within this year, ...... junks with a capacity of 150
tons each may be built.
4. Public utility office: head office established
in Singapore on October 12th with branch offices in
various places in Malaya and Sumatra. Besides building
warehouses in Singapore harbor, these public utility
offices will also undertake to build roads and bridges.
5. Broadcasting administration: This office was
established on November 24th in Singapore and controls
radio stations in various places. Work is being con-
eentrated on publicity.
6. Bailway administration: this was established
at Kualalumpur on November 25 and controls all the
railways

=== Page 172 === (confidence 0.99)
-3-
railways in Malaya and Sumatra. There are three branch
offices in Sumatra, but they have not yet started work
because of the non-arrival of personnel.
7. Observatory - will be established soon.
4.
Bus Line Connecting Peiping and Parhsien:
Peiping. Since starting the work in the spring of
194l, a lo0-kilometer bus line connecting Peiping and
Parhsien was completed within a year's time. The work
of building a 3o0-kilometer bus line between Pahsien
and Tehsien was started in April of this year and will

5.
Railway to be Constructed across sumatra.
Singapore, Dec. llth. Practically all the communica-
tion organizations in the South Seas have resumed
functioning. It is now being planned to construct a
railway traversing Sumatra. Construction will be started
in the western part of the island. Sumatra is the largest
uncultivated land in the South Seas. Furthermore, the
island has resources to meet the majority of the items
required by Japan for ensuring production power for
national defense. In Central Sumatra, a very rich coal
mine has recently been discovered, and mining work will
soon be commenced, The completion of the railway will
link Malaya and sumatra both militarily and economically.
6.
Petroleum Monopoly Law:
Tokyo, Dec. l2th. The principles of the Petroleum
Monopoly Law have been decided upon in the cabinet meeting
on December loth and are as follows:
1. Potroloum monopoly shall be placed in the hands
of the governmont which shall prescribe the different
kinds of petroleum products.
2. Petroleum manufacturers shall deliver their
petroleum products to the government which shall handle
the purchase thereof.
3. Exportation and importation of petroleum shall
be governed by government orders.
4. Petroleum sale shall be restricted to consumers
designated by the government.
5. Imposition of taxes on petroleum in Japan shall
be governed by the National Taxation Law.
7.
Produotion of Dry Cocoanut in Philippines:
Manila, Dee. l7th. In view of the increased demand
on exportation of dry cocoanut, the Military Administration
in P. I. has decided to increase the production of this
food. Conorete plans have been made as follows:
1. Replenishment

=== Page 173 === (confidence 0.99)
-4-
1. Roplenishment of labor in area of production:
The dry-cocoanut producing areas are ordinarily the
regions where food production is insufficient. In
rice-harvest time every year, the farmers of these
regions usually go to the rice fields to render help
in harvesting rice and to get rice in return as
compensation and then transport rice back to their
homes. The present is the season when a labor in-
sufficiency is felt in these places. Thus the Military
Administration Office has decided to gather together
the unemployed labor of Manila area and send them to
the dry-cocoanut producing areas to render help on
production. The first batch of labor has already been
sent.
2. Establishment of cooperatives for dry-cocoanut
production: South of Luzon, 30 villages will first be
designated for increasing production. In these villages,
cooperatives will be established, with the chief of
village in charge of the function of a cooperative. A
Commission for Increasing Production will be established
among the farmers and, as to the labor sent from Manila,
40 will be sent to each village in order to render help.
Up to now, l2 cooperatives have already been established
in these regions.
3. Technical guidance for increasing production:
100 experts having experiences in production of dry-
cocoanut will be selected and sent out to all the areas
of production for making inspections periodically in
order to increase production.
4. Control of distribution of raw cocoanut: In
view of the increased consumption of raw cocoanut in
the Manila area and the fact that its prices are even
higher than those for dry cocoanut, it has been decided
to have the Food Control Office and Dry-Cocoanut Purchase
Office take joint steps to fix proper prices for raw
cocoanut in areas of production. A minimum quantity of
purchase has been set in order to adjust the control of
supply and demand in Manila.
8.
Ship-building Program in Hongkong:

Japanese Trade Group Law:
Japan, Jan. 23rd. The Japanese Trade Group Law was
promulgated on January 22. Following are the important
articles of this law:
Chapter I. General Regulations.
Art. 1. The Trade Group shall exercise control over
the trading of commodities with the object of strengthen-
ing the total economic force of the nation and maintaining
sufficient stocks of materials and guaranteeing the proper
use of these materials.
Art. 2. The Business Office shall be established at
Tokyo. Business Offices may be established also at points
considered as necessary with Government's approval.
Art. 3. The capital shall be 300 million yen made up of
3 million shares of lo0 yen each. This capital may be
increased with Government's approval.
Art. 5. The Government will invest in the Trade Group
a sum of 350 million yen.
Art. 2l. The functions of the Trade Group shall be:
(1) Export and Purchase of Materials.

Tax Increases in Japan:
Japan, Jan. 17th. The Government has decided to
lay stress on indirect taxes in order to promote thrift.
The outline of this law was passed in the Cabinet
Conference on the 15th and the essential items of tax
inoroases were promulgated on the following day as
follows:
1. Wine tax and cold drink tax show an increase
of about loo% in the total amount of tax revenues.
However, a fixed amount will be supplied to one who
works at increasing the production of important materials
at the prices prevailing before the increase of taxes.
2. Touring, Food and Drink Taxes will be increased
30 to 200 per cent from their present rates of 90 to
l00 per cent. The rate of inerease in taxes on dwelling,
anchoring, eteetere, will be lowered.

special attention is paid to the maintenance of the
livelihood of the nationals. Consumption of luxuries is
charged the highest rates. Taxes on commodities which
can be consumed less are also raised. It is anticipated
that the tax revenues in the 1?43 fiscal year will thus
show an increase of l000 million yen.
4. Cigarette prices will be raised. The rates of

43%, averaging 6l. It is estimated that the increase

Hainan Island Conditions:
Fukuoka, Jan. 20th. The administrative officer of
Hainan returned to Japan on the 19th. Following is his
talk on the latest conditions of that island:
Since the occupation of that island, the authorities
have been endeavoring to promote the industries and
increase the food production of that place. This island
will gain self-sufficiency in rice this crop year. If
the arts of farming could be improved, the production
would be increased to three times the present amount.
In the l943 crop year, much attention will also be paid
to marine and animal products. Recently an animal
products stockshare company has been established. This
company aims at increasing the production of cattle and
swine. There are two companies dealing in the aquatic
products business. Both of them are rather successful.
5.
Plans for Building Wooden Vessels:
Japan, Jan. lOth. The Board of Sea Affairs aims at
quick building of wooden vessels. The outline of
emergency plans for building wooden vessels formulated
by this Board was passed in the Cabinet Meeting on the
20th and will be made effective as from the beginning of
the l943-44 fiscal year. The chief points of this outline
are: To readjust the usual 5 standard wartime types and
limit them to 3 kinds, i.e. 250 gross tons, 150 gross tons
and l00 gross tons. At the same time attempts will be
made to build iron and wooden boats of 300 and 500 gross
tons in order to increase the size gradually in future.
Mueh will also be done to simplify the construction of the
vessel as much as possible. Studies will also be made to
facilitate quick mass production.

German Bank in Japan:
Based upon the Japan-Germany Economic Cooperation
Pact, Germany will very soon established a German East
Asiatic Bank at Tokyo, to be capitalized at 40,000,000
marks. Japan has already had a bank in Berlin, i.e.
the Yokohama Specie Bank. Hereafter in the final
settlement of accounts between Germany and Japan, the
yen-mark cross rate snall be based upon, instead of
basing upon the American dollar as before.
8.
Formosan Rice in malaya:
Singapore, Jan. 2lst. The Government of Penang
has recently decided to purchase 4,500 acress of land
for planting Formosan water-rice, as a trial. Trial
planting of rice in Alosta Area has achieved great
success.
9.
Commerce Between the P.I. and Shanghai:
Manila, Jan. 23rd. The Military and Political
Headquarters of the P.I. have been arran ing the
exchange of materials between the P.I. and Shanghai.
It is decided that the P.1. should transport to
Shanghai copra and sugar while Shanghai should ship
back cotton textiles, paper and cigarettes. The first
and second shipments are to leave Shanghai in succession
very soon. Negotiations for concluding a pact relating
to the exchange of all kinds of materials are still in
progress.

Economic Items Selected From:
Radio Broadcasts of the Japanese and the Nanking Regime
as monitored and released by the Ministry of Information.
(Period January 23, 1943 - February 3, l943; abstracts

1.
Prices Control in Shanghai:
Shanghai, Jan. 23rd. In view of the upward
tendency of commodity prices, the Shanghai Municipal
Council of the International Settlement has adopted
strict measures for keeping down prices. On January 23,
a proclamation was promulgated to the following effect:
As from January 23, 1943, the prices of commodities
belonging to producers or wholesale merchants shall be
under the control of the Shanghai Municipal Council.
No producers and/or wholesale merchants shall raise
prices above the level on January 23, l943, without
permission of the authorities. The producer or whole-
sale merchant shall submit a statement to the Shanghai
Municipal Council giving the January 23, 1943 prices
and calculations showing how these prices are derived,
not later than February loth.
2.
State Control of Iron Factories:
Japan, Jan. 27th. For the purpose of increasing
the production of iron which is the basic material for
carrying on the war, the Ministry of Commerce and
Industry brings the important iron factories in Japan
under its control through the issuance of an ordinance
based upon the National General Mobilization Law. In
the morning of the 27th instant, representatives of
the various factories were summoned to the Office of
the Minister where the ordinance was handed to them.
It is pointed out that the state control of important
factories was started last May when radium factories
were placed under government control. This is the
second time at which state control is applied. What
will be placed under special control is the distribution
of materials, labor and power. Controlling officers
will be stationed at the various factories to give
directions with the object of increasing the efficiency
of productive work.
3.
War Prisoners Employed:
Japan, Jan. 27th. According to the Chief of the
War Prisoners Information Bureau who just returned from
a trip through Japan Proper (not including Formosa),
Korea and Hokkaido for the inspection of the war prisoners
in those places, American, British and Dutch war prisoners
below the rank of colonel are all doing some sort of work
to assist in the increase of production. They actually
work

=== Page 190 === (confidence 0.99)
-6-
work for us. However, due to causes relating to food
and environments, they can not compare with Japanese
laborers in efficiency. Their working efficiency is
generally only 60-70 per cent of that of the Japanese.
The Chief is of opinion that the promotion of their
working efficiency will depend much upon the directions
of the keepers. In a certain dockyard in Kyushu, a
considerable number of prisoners are working side by
side with Japanese laborers. Their working efficiency
is found to be not much different from that of the
Japanese. This is owing to the attention paid by the
dockyard to the prisoners' health, skill and ability.
The war prisoners all have a good living and are grateful
to the Japanese.
4.
Kwangtung Coal-mining:
Canton, Jan. 27th. The Board of Reconstruction of
the Provincial Government now commences large-scaled
coal-mining. They are now conducting the drilling of
the coal mines in Hwa Hsien. On the 25th instant, the
Highost Commander in South China inspected 3 coal mines
located in Panyu and Hwa Hsien.
5.
Silk Manufacturing Amalgamation:
Japan, Jan. 29th. In the spring of 194l, the silk
industry of our country (Japan) was reorganized and as
a result the equipment was reduced from 210,000 pans
(for boiling cocoons) to l00,O00 pans. The silk
situation thereafter ... ... (interrupted). Now a big
silk manufacturing company will be formed to amalgamate
all the silk factories. The capital is learned to
range from 150 million yen to 200 million yen. Its
development is being closely watched by the general
public.
6.
Labor Shortage:
Shanghai, Jan. 29th. Chinese laborers in Central
China with Shanghai as the center are gradually shifting
to important industries due to the participation of war
by the National Government. From the viewpoint of
economic eooperation between Japan, Manchuria and China,
they should go to Manchuria and North China where a
shortage of labor is being felt. Since the lst moon
(lunar calendar), it is believed that there has been a
brisk flow of laborers. Every year North China and
Manchuria get a considerable supply of labor from Shanghai,
comprising workmen trained in ship-building and mechanical
work and general coolies. For the purpose of reviving
the industries in Central China, the National Government
and the Japanese Embassy impose restrictions on the supply
of labor to outports. However, in the case of Manohuria,
the number of laborers to emigrate there has been fixed
in a pact concluded at the end of last year. In the case
of North China and Kwantung Province (Kwantung Leased
Territory with Dairen), the authorities have recently held

=== Page 191 === (confidence 0.99)
-7-
a conference concerning labor problems. Such affairs
as the wages of the laborer, travelling expenses and
enrollment, are to be decided by the authorities
concerned. It is now hoped by all that laborers from
Central China will be supplied to the various areas
in the coprosperity sphere in large numbers.
7.
Coal-Mining in Manchuria:
Hsinking (Changchun), Jan. 28th. The coal produc-
tion in Manchuria started to show marked increase in
1942. In December 1942 the amount of coal diggings in
the whole of Manchuria reached more than l20 per cent
of the amount projected.

8.
Repairs of Railways in Java:
Hongkong, Jan. 30th. The trunk line of Java's
railway and the iron bridge in eastern Java (measuring
150 meters) have recently been completed. With this,
all the iron bridges in Java have been restored. The
Military and Political Headquarters of Java is calling
the first meeting of the chiefs of overland transporta-
tion bureau with the object of increasing overland
transportation facilities.
9.
Tax Revenue of National Government:
Shanghai, Jan. 30th. The expenditures of the
National Government have been on a rapid increase since
participation of war. In the first Supreme National
Defence Conference held last year, it was estimated that
the annual expenditures would total 600 million yen.
The Ministry of Finance must develop the resources of
wealth and at the same time to maintain the livelihood
of the people. Therefore it has decided to reorganize
the financial structure with the object of effecting a
natural increase in the tax revenues. The reorganization
of financial structure was carried out on the lst of
January this year and in addition, customs duties, salt
taxes, consolidated taxes were raised by way of levying
taxes according to value instead of quantity. The
projected amount of revenues during the lst half of this
year 1s CRB$340,473,000, showing a substantial increase
over the amount collected during the corresponding
period last year. The principal tax revenues projected

10.
Southssas Situation:
Japan, Feb. lst.
Economic Development: Although much destruction
could not be avoided, repairs were quickly made to
factories so that important materiels for national
defence

=== Page 192 === (confidence 0.99)
-8-
dofence will be ours. Much will depend upon transporta-

in ships.
Kerosene Oil: Factories repaired, about % (not
given). It is estimated that by the end of 1943 all
the installations will be fully restored, and by that
time transportation will also show great improvement.
Mineral Resources: What Japan expects from the
Southseas are iron, alumina, copper, manganese, pewter,
aluminum, etcetera. Most of the mines were destroyed
artificially but repairs were quickly effected. The
production of alumina has even exceeded the prewar
level. The obtaining of kerosene oil, iron and alumina
by Japan means the strengthening of the foundation of
Japanese air force. The destruction to manganese mines
was considerable, but with the strenuous efforts of our
industrial circles, mining was resumed in October last.
The production of lead has reached the pre-war level.
The pewter mines in Manila and Banga are famous in the
world. Since their occupation, the pewter works have
been supplying the requirements of Japan.
Agricultural Resources: Rubber, coconut forests,
quinine, sugar, etcetera, are produced in large quantities.
Efforts must be exerted toward the expansion of the
production of rubber and lubricating oil. The sugar
produced in P. I. and Java is enough to meet the total
needs of the Greater Eastern Asia. The P. I. are paying
much attention to the expansion of cotton production.
Foodstuffs: The food requirements of  the South
areas, military and civilians, will be met with the
local production as much as possible. Efforts are being
made towards the interchange of materials between
different areas, the large-scale expansion of production,
and the use of substitutes, with very good results. The
Malay Islands'production of rice is only sufficient to
meet one-third of their requirements. It is planned to
transport a certain quantity from Java into that area,
besides promoting local production, enforcing curtailment
of consumption and increasing imports. There is surplus
in Java of rice and other cereals for exportation. The
rice export surplus of Burma is very large. It is being
studied how to store the product besides exporting it to
other areas. The riee deficit of the P.I. is not large;
it is estimated that it will soon attain a state of self-
sufficiency with the present promotion of production.
Communications: The military forces, since the
outbreak of war, hava been utilizing the requisitioning
of vessels to assist in the transportation of materials.
The reconstruction of the South areas contributes much
to the Greater Eastern Asiatic War. Therefore, the
military forces there are steadily increasing the overseas
transportation facilities. ... ... (interrupted).

1.
Wooden Vessels Between Canton and Formosa:
Canton, Feb. 6th. The Provincial Government of
Kwangtung will in the near future establish the
Canton Transportation Company to open navigation
between Canton and Taiwan (Formosa), whereby the
goods accumulated in Canton can be shipped to Taiwan
for consumption, and on the return trip, Formosan
glutinous rice and coal which are required by Canton
can be shipped back. The plan has already been
established and speedy preparations are being made
for its realization. The operation will be undertaken
by the Provincial Government's Board of Reconstruction
while the business department will be handled by the
shipping companies of Japan.
2.
Conditions in the malaya States:
Nanking (?), Feb. 12th. According to a mossage
from Singapore, the Japanese military and political
officer stated, in answer to a news correspondent,
although shipping space is short the important
materials, iron, alumina, tin, coconut oil and rubber
are exported to Japan in quantities sufficient to
meet the requirements in Japan Proper.
In response to a question as to the results of the
plans during the past year for increasing the production
of foodstuffs, the officer stated the rice production
this crop year showed a 20 per cent increase, and in
the next crop year the increase may reach 50 per cent.
The crops of subsidiary foodsturfs including tapioca in
different localities have also made extraordinary progress.
Efforts are being exerted towards the expansion of the
production of these subsidiary foodstuffs to supplement
the rice deficit. The expsnsion of the production of
fiber crops, such as cotton, flax, etcetera, is being
initiated in Southern Sumatra. With regard to overseas
transportation, due success has been achieved in the first
salvage of sunken vessels. The Building of wooden vessels
is being steadily pushed and it is estimated that by the
end of March this year a considerably large number of
these vessels will be launched and by the end of June there
will

=== Page 195 === (confidence 0.99)
-2-
will be still more speedy progress. The shortage of
transportation facilities shall be remedied as soon
as possible. Branches of the Yokohama Specie Bank
have been opened in the important cities. The banks
belonging to oversea Chinese and Indians have also
been re-opened.
3。
Japanese Commercial Minister Reports on Cotton Cuestion:
Japan, Feb. 15th. In answer to a question on
cotton, the Commercial Minister stated on the 15th in
the House of Commons that due to the shortage of cotton
supply to meet the requirements of the whole co-
prosperity sphere, a free utilization will be made
of other fibers, such as chemical fiher, rayon, silk,
flax, etcetera. Plans are being formulated for the
expansion of the production of all kinds of fibers,
especially cotton. In North and Central China, the
cotton produced there may meet the cotton requirements
of the various areas in the co-prosperity sphere. The
expansion of china's cotton production is therefore
the foremost mission of tne country. at the same time,
the acreage usuelly planted to sugarcane in the Philippines
is being shifted to cotton and steps are also being taken
to develop cotton cultivation in the other southsea areas.
However, it is still advisable to attach importance to
that in North and Central Chine. Therefore it is very
important to supply the cotton producers there with
foodstuffs and pay them a suitable purchase price for
cotton.
The Commercial Minister explained the policy of
collecting materials from occupied areas in China.
According to him, there is no question about the
importation of iron ores and coal into Japan from China,
inasmuch as the production of these materials are
controlled by the Japanese. However, there is much
difficulty in the purchasing of cotton and other farm
products which are produced by the Chinese people.
Measures for coping with the Chinese conditions regarding
prices, collection, development, etcetera, should be
planned from the viewpoint of increasing the Japanese
fighting strength.
4.
Review of Economic Reconstruction in the Malaya States

Singapore, Feb. 14th. On the lst anniversary of
the fall of Singapore, an annual review of the economic

follows:
Industrial Reconstruction: The fundamental policy
aims at self-surficiency in foodstuffs. Because Malaya's
principal production is that of tin and rubber, this
area depended in prewar years upon oversea imports for
its supply of foodstuffs, the domestio produetion being
only sufficient to meet 4% of local consumption. Plans
were initiated a year ago for the expansion of foodstuffs
in

placed under the management of the said Federation
and carried out very smoothly. Although over-production
is still witnessed, this problem can suitably be solved
by finding outlets in consumin& centers. In addition,
Malaya and Sumatra are very rich in the resources of
special Southseas products. With regard to these
products, plans have also been formulated for increasing
their production according to the extent of requirements
of Japan Proper and abroad. Regarding cotton production
expansion, the site selected is south umatra, to co-

The officers specially commissioned for this expansion

seeds is expected to be completed and the first harvest
will be reaped in September.

all resumed activities. These banks all exerted efforts
toward the absorption of the floating capital and the
investment in the development of resources. In April

all banks in Maleya and Sumatra whereby the banks have

been the slightest sign of the appearance of currency

of materials between the South areas.

5.
North China Production:
Peking, Feb. 6th. The Director of the North China
Development Company made the following statements during
a conference of the Company held on the 15th:
Coal: The coal production has shown an increase of
50-60% over the prewar level. 59 per cent is consumed
locally and 36 per cent exported to Japan, Manchuria and
Central China.
Iron: The mines at Lungyen in Mongolia, Chinlingchen
and LIkwo in Shantung province, Shihchiaying in Hopei, and
a number of places in Shansi are being opened. At the end
of 1942 the North China Iron Works was established and
placed under the charge of the North China Development
Company. The mineral ores under the ground are abundant
and development is sure.
Other Mineral Resources: Clay, lead and other ores
are of much values to Japan, Manchuria and China. Raw
materials for manufacturing sulphate of ammonia are also
important mineral resources of North China. Last year a
North Chine Nitrate Fertilizer Company was established at
Talyuan, Shansi, and its production will in future con-
tribute much to the food and cotton crops as well as others
in North China.

Salt: The methods of getting salt in Changlu and
Shantung have been greatly improved. Salt and coal are
important products produced in North China from where
large quantities are supplied to other areas in the
GreaterEastern Asiatic co-prosperity sphere.
Cotton: The expansion of the cotton production in
North China is greatly depended upon by the rest of the
Greater Eastern Asiatic co-prosperity sphere. Redoubled
efforts are being exerted toward this end and at the
same time consideration is being given to the way of
collecting cotton for the requirements of the spinning
industry.
6.
Naval Authorities xplain Present situation and Policies:
Japan, Feb. 17th. The Japanese naval authorities
gave the following explanation of the current situation
and policies:
The policy regarding occupied areas is to effect a
quick development of the important materials for national
defence. For the purpose of prosecuting the war, it is
unavoidable that the people in the occupied areas must
suffer hardships in their economic daily life in order
that utmost efforts are made to satisfy the fighters
requirements and to maintain a good supply of materials
for national defence.
Great efforts are being exerted toward the betterment
of communication and transportation. It goes without
saying that the equipment of the various harbors must be
completed. It is also desired to expedite the building
of vessels, especially wooden ones.
There is necessity for increasing the production and
arranging the interexchange of rice in the occupied areas.
At the same time it is planned to take steps to collect
the bark of the 'Ch'eng Ka Le Mu' trees for manufacturing
substitutes for cotton. A Dried Coconut Controlling
Federation has been established to deal with the collection
of copre for export to Japan Proper and for oil extracting
locally. It is also important to deal with rubber-tree
planting affairs in Borneo.
The economic development of the Southsea areas is
based primarily upon the principle that it is of the first
importance to develop the important resources for national
defence. However, of all the outstanding problems, the
expansion of transportation facilities is the most urgent.
In the following the leading industries or enterprises are
briefly discussed:
(1) Equipment relating to kerosene oil industry was
greatly destroyed by the Allied enemy. However, since
our occupation, speedy restoration has been brought about
by strenuous efforts. Up to the end of last year, the
Sanga-Sanga and Tarakan oil fields in Borneo were able to
produce oil. Those in Ceram have been restored to their
old status, with a portion of them producing oil. A survey
of

=== Page 200 === (confidence 0.99)
-6-
of the oil fields at Tanyo (?) in Borneo was completed
in December 1942 and preparations are being made for
their development. The Balik Papan (?) Oil Refinery is
known to all. By relentless efforts toward repairing,
this refinery is producing oil at its full capacity.
(2) The coal production of Borneo will hereafter
play an important part in the development of the South.
The coal mines at Lantanpanchen (?) and Nokoor (?) have
been repaired and are producing.
(3) Development of the nickel mines in the Celebes
has been steadily carried out. at prese t, this product
is exported to Japan Iroper in & considerable volume.
(4) Cotton-cultivation is very hopeful in the Celebes.
In the vicinity of menaad, about ,suo cho (1 cho equals
2.45 acres) were planted to cotton this crop year and the
hervest was of very good quality. It is decided that in
the next crop year formal cultivation will be commenced
and plans will be formulated for tne gradual annual expan-
sion of production.
(5) Surveys of mineral resources, agriculture and
forestry, marine products, etcetera, of an emergency
nature are being made in Celebes, Borneo and Ceram as well
as in New Guinea. By the end of last year restoration of
these regions to their former status was generally completed.
The building of wooden vessels is being pushed. There are
eleven ship-building docks. It is planned to build during
1943-44 a considerable number of 150-ton to 500-ton wooden
vessels to assume the oversea transportation of materials
from these places to Japan Iroper. The materials include
nickel, copra, raw rubber, kapok, etcetera.  network of
bus routes is being planned, due to the importance of
maintaining peace and order as well as the development
of these places. although some routes are already opened
to traffic, they are not yet deemed sufficient.
(6) Those persons who have been, or are being sent
there are mostly experts for the extracting of resources
for our national defence. It is also deemed necessary to
despatch a number of industrial and commercial professionals
of the middle or low class to complete the entire economic
structure. These will be able to conduct an actual survey
of these places.
(7) In the central, eastern and northern coastal
regions of New Guinea, there are rich deposits of mineral
resources while in the whole area, forests are abundant.
However, present efforts are focused on the attainment of
self-sufficienoy in foodstuffs.
7.
Reconstruction of Hongkong:
Hongkong, Feb. 2oth. The present conditions in regard
to the reconstruotion of Hongkong are given hereunder:
Trade: Hongkong is regarded as a middle link in the
co-prosperity sphere. The South China Economic Conference
now being held in Canton has as one of its main problems
for

=== Page 201 === (confidence 0.99)
-7-
for discussion "How to utilize Hongkong, the Middle
Linking Harbor." The Governor of Hongkong has now
leased part of the warehouses under its management to
eight shipping companies. These companies, in turn,
established on February l8th a warehouse-operating
joint office with the object of doing their utmost to
utilize the facilities of the harbor. In October l942
a Trade Pact was signed with the P. I. whereby necessary
materials will be imported. since then efforts have
been exerted toward increasing the flow of materials
between this island and the Southseas, as well as with
different Chinese areas.
Shipbuilding and Oversea Transportation: The
equipment of shipbuilding docks at longkong is the best
in the co-prosperity sphere. opeedy restoration to their
former status has now been accomplished. Up to the
present, (number omitted) large-sized new freighters have
been completed. The results of tne repairing docks are
also excellent. almost all of the sunken vessels in the
harbor have been salved. These, after due repairs, can
be put into operation again. Recently wooden vessels
with modern propelling machinery have been built. The
first fleet were launched in January. In February it is
estimated that (number omitted) more will be launched.
These wooden vessels are for transporting goods between
Hongkong and the Southseas. It is planned to sail these
vessels between Hongkong and Canton and Swatow, and later
to supplement the steamship service between Hongkong and
French Indo-China.
Industry: The manufacturing inaustries of Manila-
hemp tobacco, oxygen, cement, beer, cold drinks, food-
stuffs, sugar and so on are all handled by Japanese under
the control of the Government-General. The latter has
recently promulgated its policy of transferring the
factories under its management to the people and requiring
these factories to answer the needs of Hongkong by produc-
ing necessary materials. For example, the beer brewery
shall shift part of its equipment from beer to alcohol
production.  Chinese-operated factories that have been
permitted to be re-opened number more than 700, including
those relating to fibers and foodstuffs.
Population: Since Japanese occupation of Hongkong,
the Government-General has been persuading Chinese residents
to move out and is affording them shipping facilities. It
is estimated that about 900,000 people have been thus sent
out. This policy will be continued and negotiations are
being held with the authorities in Kwangtung Province for
admitting these people.
8.
Plans for Industry in China:
Shanghai, Feb. 2Oth. The Shanghai Office of the
Japanese Embassy announced to the news correspondents the
following:
The policy of Japan is to increase the fighting
strength of the National Government, at the same time,
giving consideration to the people's economic conditions.

Heavy industries, such as iron production, ship-

that the Japanese spinning industry will be moved to
the Continent. The spinning industry in Central
China has been somewhat affected by the shortage of
raw material.
Japan (?), Feb. 23rd. During a meeting of the
North China Development Commission in the House of
Commons on the 24th the Chief of the Fiber Bureau
made the following statements:
The clothing requirements of the South, Manchuria
and Mongolia are large. There is little surplus in
Japan proper. The present clothing policy of the
Government aims at the maintenance of the supply of
fibers. It is hoped that the cotton production in
North China will reach l0 million piculs in the future.
However, the present production is only several million
piculs. Efforts are being made towards its expansion.
Cotton cultivation is also being taken up in the South.
Experts have been despatched there to increase the
production. With regard to the removal of fiber
industries to the Continent, studies are being made
into the local living conditions, labor and transporta-
tion.

Repairs to the Grand Canal and Yellow River Dykes:
Yangchow, Feb. 2lst. The River Conservancy Commission
has decided to establish, in Northern Kiangsu, an office
of works for repairing the embankment guarding the Grand
Canel. It is learned that engineering work will be started
in a few days.

=== Page 203 === (confidence 0.99)

Nanking, Feb. 24th. The Ministry of Reconstruc-

Kaifeng, Feb. 25th. The only new reconstruction
undertaking of Honan is the building of the embankment
guarding the new Yellow River. This year's work will
be started on March lst and end on June 30th. It is
estimated that within these four months 800,000 people
will be mobilized and the funds expended will amount to
several million dollars (F.P.B.). The embankment will
start from Shihchiao Village in Chungmou Hsien and end
at Nansungkang in Taikang Hsien, totalling 75 km in
length. People living outside the River Valley will
also be required to supply labor and funds.

Consumption of Sweet Potatoes:
Peking, Feb. 23rd. In view of a shortage of dried
sweet potato slices, the Municipal Government has trans-
ported to Peking large quantities of this produce. The
wholesale price is set at F.R.B.$lo0 per lo0 catties and
the retail price at l.20 per catty.
Japan, Feb. 23rd. During a session of the House
of Nobles on the 22nd, the Minister of Agriculture and
Forestry made the following statements in answer to
questions raised by other members:
It is planned to curtail imports of foreign rice
this crop year. For attaining self-sufficiency in food-
stuffs, sweet potatoes, potatoes, miscellaneous grains
and Manchurian soybeans will be rationed. In case of
poor harvests, the deficit will be made up from old
stocks of foreign rice.
The price of wheat is the same as that of third
grade rice at present; the ratio is very well balanced.
The projected i943 production of sweet potatoes is
1,800 million kan, an increase of l00% over the original
figure.
Canton, Feb. 25th. The Municipal Government promul-
gated on the 20th the regulations of using miscellaneous
foodstuffs for human consumption. In these regulations
it is stipulated that every person, whether officer or
ordinary people, shall eat a certain quantity of sweet
potatoes every day.
Suchow, Feb. 26th. with a view to increasing produc-

have been issued to the effect that the people should
plant and eat as many sweet potatoes as possible.

Agricultural and Mulberry Experiment Stations at Ningpo:
Shanghai, Feb. 5th. According to a correspondent
in Ningpo, the Administrative Office to Eastern Chekiang
Province will establish agricultural and mulberry
experiment stations with the object of increasing
production. Instructions have been given to the effect
that preparations for their establishment must be
completed not later than the end of March this year.
Production of kerosene in China:
Nanking (?), Feb. 8th. In response to a question
raised by
, during the meeting of the kerosene
Monopoly Law Commission hela at the House of Commons,
the Minister of Commerce and Industries gave the
following explanation:
North China is very rich in coal. It is hoped to
initiate an artificial kerosene enterprise there.
Therefore steps have been taken to make studies about
the utilization of coal for the manufacturing of
artificial kerosene oil. The only question is that it
requires a large-scale equipment and much labor and
technical skill. It is therefore not advisable to start
the great enterprise right now. At present studies are
being made into the quality of coal and other affairs
in preparation for starting work in future as it is
deemed that there is a possibility for the conditions to
develop to that stage.
Large Quantities of Pig Iron from Manchuria:
Japan, Feb. lOth. Since the outbreak of the Greater
Eastern Asiatic War, "Manchukuo" has been assisting Japan
as much as possible, especially in the supply of pig iron.
The quota of pig iron export to Japan set for the produc-
tion year 1942-43 was fulfilled on February 6th, or two
months before the time limit. Japan is also satisfied
with the production plan for the new production year.
Indo-China's Custom Duty Policy Toward Japan:
Japan, Feb. l4th. In response to a question raised
by Kawakami during the session of the House of Commons
on the 13th, Yamaguchi, Chief of the Commercial and
Industrial Trade Bureau stated that after the obtaining
of customs autocracy from France, the French Indo-China
Government adopted a two-fold system in fixing its customs
tariff

=== Page 205 === (confidence 0.99)
-11-
tariff - a general customs tariff and a tariff of the
lowest rates. In the case of Japan, which is the
signatory of the Japan-French lndo-China Pact, the
tariff of the lowest rates applies. The rates are
equal to only one-third of these in tne general customs
tariff. with regard to the foodstuffs and other daily
necessities imported from Japan totalling 47 items,
the duties are exempted. The rates of duty imposed on
cotton piece goods and miscellaneous articles are even
lower than the lowest rates fixed. Such articles as
corn, coal, castor oil, etcetera for export to Japan
are also exempted from duty payment.
The Great Importance of North China:
Japan, Feb. l8th. It was questioned by somebody
during a session of the House of Nobles as to whether
North China has lost part of its importance with the
procuration of the resources in the South. To this,
an explanation was given as follows:
If North China is excluded, the construction of
the co-prosperity sphere will be hopeless. This is
because North China has coal deposits reaching about
2,Ooo million tons. The coke and anthracite produced
there are indispensable materials in our iron industry.
The salt production is also rich and indispensable to
our chemical industry. The quality of smoked iron (?)
1s above 50% and its deposits are also abundant. The
electricity-generating power of the Yellow River and
the fertilizer industry, if successful, will contribute
much to the expansion of the production of foodstuffs
and cotton. For these reasons, North China is still a
very important region to us.

Reference underlying communication
from Roy Hoko Ikeda.
Mr. keda's communicatior 1s primarily
devoted to proposels for post-war reorganiza-
tion in the Japanese governmentel, economic
and social structure. The basic aim is
1mprovement of conditions of the people
and giving them a real voice in government.
Mr. Ikeda's suggestions include a
reformation of the status of the Emperor
who should be reduced to the status of a
mortal. The Emperor would have the power
of approval and veto but would exercise
his power to govern through his cabinet.
Regarding territorial possessions the
writer proposes: Japen should retain the
economic possessions acquired by legal
means 1n Manchuria and other occupied areas.
Korea and Formosa should be given limited
self-government and the right to elect
representatives to the National Diet in
order that these colonies might help
eradicate Japanese imperialiem. After a
certain time these colonies would decide
their own status by a plebiscite. Japan
should endeavor to purchase Saghalien from
Russia.
Mr. Ikeda

=== Page 218 === (confidence 0.97)
DEPARTMENT OF STATE
DIVISION OF FAR EASTERN AFFAIRS
-2-
Mr. Ikeda makes the following pro-
posals regarding other areas in the Far
East: The East Indies, Malaye, Burma
and Indochina should be self-governing
under the trusteeship of their mother
countries. India should have its own
Hong
government under dominion status.
The
Kong should be returned to China.
"southeastern erohipelago which is
possessed by America and Japan should
be amalgamated to the Philippines". All
of the foregoing semi-colonial countries
must eventually be given full independence.
Internationally the writer proposes
regional councils and an international
government whose powers would include
international policing power.

closure to despatch No. 1049 of April 5, 1943, from
the American Embassy, Chungking, China, to the Department
of State on the subject: "Economic Material from

Economic Items Selected From:
Radio Broadcasts of the Japanese and the Nanking Regime
as monitored and released by the Ministry of Information.
(Translated by 3. Y. Feng for the period March 1, 1943,
to March 10, 1943; abstracts transmitted in Embassy's
telegram No. 355, March 11, 1943, 8 p.m.)
1.
Shanghai Food Conditions:
Shanghai, Mar. 2nd. The Japanese Consul General
has remarked as follows:
Food problem is one of the most important problems
of Shanghai. We should try our best for its betterment.
Great assistance has been rendered by the military, and
the amount of rice rationed to the Chinese has shown an
increase. At present the ration is 6 kilograms of rice
and 2t kilograms of flour per capita, per week. This
shows that the food problem has been solved.
The Commodity Price problem is also important.
The Shanghai Office of the Embassy is trying hard to
find out the causes for the rises and remedial measures
will be applied. It is anticipated that in near future
this problem will be solved. However, due to the
complex nature of this problem, we cannot hope for a
speody solution. According to studies made by the
Shanghai Office, the prices of principal daily necessi-
ties on February 5, l943, when compared with those on
May 31, l937, have shown considerable inereases. This
has seriously affected the general public and should be
remedied as soon as possible.
Shanghai, Mar. 7th. With the recent skyrocketing
of commodity prices, much anxiety has boen aroused
among the inhabitants over their living. Those in the
civil service are especially hard hit. With a view to
lessening their hardships the Municipal Government is
organizing cooperatives for them.
2.
Current Japanese Crop Plans:
Japan, Mar. 5th. With regard to projected produc-
tion of staple foodstuffs for the l943-44 crop year,
the statements repeatedly made by Ino, Minister of
Agriculture and Forestry, during sessions of the present
Diet are summarized in the following:
The projected production of rice is about the same
as that for the preceding crop year, being more than 71
million koku.
The projected production or, wheat, barley snd naked
barley shows a slight decrease.
The

=== Page 234 === (confidence 0.97)
-2-
The goals of production of sweet potatoes and
potatoes have been greatly raised, with an increase
of about lo0 million kan in sweet potato production
over last year's goal, bringing the projected
production to more than 1,760 million kan and an
inerease of about 25 million kan in the production
of potatoes, bringing the goal to more than 780
million kan. The increase will be effected principally
through the improvement of the art of cultivation,
whereby the present average yield of 350 kan (per 0.1
cho ?) is expected to be increased to 800 kan.
The lowering of the goal of production of wheat,
barley and naked barley has been decided in view of the
supply of fertilizers and in view of the results
obtained in the preceding crop year. with regard to
the production of such products as furnish protein and
fats - soybeans, fish, etcetera, the preceding crop
year's goals are generally maintained. The projected
production of corn has been raised 45,000 koku higher.
With the shortage of fertilizer and labor for the
current crop year, the principle is to maintain constant
production of the principal grains, i.e. rice, wheat,
otcetera, and at the same time to bring about marked
increases in the production of products requiring little
fertilizer such as potatoes and sweet potatoes, in order
to fulfill the wartime food requirements. In the
following the goals of the production of farm products
for the current crop year are given with comparisons
of the preceding season's figures:

3.
Report on the Southseas Region:
Japan, Mar. 6th. The Southseas Section of the
Greater Eastern Asia Ministry gave an explanation,
during a session of the House of Commons on the 6th
instant, regarding the present situation of agriculture
and forestry, animal husbandry, etcetera in the Southseas
areas and future plans as follows:
The plan for assuring the expansion of fiber produc-
tion is being carried out smoothly. It is expected that
self-sufficfency in these products can be attained.
In

=== Page 235 === (confidence 0.99)
-3-
In order to avoid an abrupt economic change in
those areas, it is not proposed to forcibly restrict
the production of such materials which leave surpluses.
From the viewpoint of economizing the consumption
of important materials, we have adopted the policy of
encouraging the local processing of animal and marine
products as much as possible.
The agricultural policy attaches importance to
the supply of materials which are found to be in-
sufficient in the coprosperity sphere. However,
consideration must also be given to the important
problem concerning those products in the coprosperity
sphere the production of which leads in the whole
world or even supplies surpluses. In order to avoid a
curtailment of their production, it will be necessary
to develop new outlets as well as to expand their local
consumption.
Those materials which are found most insufficient
are fibers, especially cotton. The fiber deficit in
the areas under Japanese control is very large. Strenuous
efforts, therefore, are being exerted toward the expansion
of the production of cotton, ramie and hemp. The results
are satisfactory and a certain degree of self-sufficiency
has been attained.
There are considerable surpluses of coconut oil
(椰子油),palm oil (棕櫚]油)，copra oil (椰核油)，etcetera.
It is therefore necessary to seek new uses of these oils
and new methods of disposing of them locally. Although
a surplus of sugar is also left, fortunately it can be
used as raw material for manufacturing ether ( ) (?)
and alcohol (酒 精). Local sugar mills are gradually
shifting their efforts toward this direction. However,
it is probably unavoidable that the sugar production may
have to be curtailed to a certain extent in the whole
territory.
With regard to such medicines as quinine (規 那),
perhaps it may be said that the present production is
not yet sufficient owing to the increasing importance of
such products. We have not only tried to increase their
production but also to seek for new uses.
With regard to the supply of foodstuffs, there is
no deficit as yet in the Greater Eastern Asiatic co-
prosperity sphere as a whole. However, from now on,
offorts should be exerted toward the attainment of self-
sufficiency in the respective areas within the sphere
separately.
The production of lumber in the South should be
expanded, espeeially the materials for making vehicles.
With regard to animal products, importanee will be
attached to the maintenance or local military supplies.
Suitable localities will be selected for their propagation
or at least for maintaining the production at the original
lovel.
In

=== Page 236 === (confidence 0.99)
-4-
In order to save transportation by ships, strenuous
offorts are being exerted toward the promotion of local
processing industries. For instance, if we ship cotton
to Japan and export it out again in the form of cloth,
it would be quite uneconomic. It would be better to
have the spinning and weaving done in the cotton produc-
ing areas. This also applies to alcohol (酒 精 ) and
ether(丁 醇) (?).

Poking Food Supplies:
Faking, Mar. 4th. In view of the fact that the
average inhabitant of the Municipality finds it difficult
to keep on with the food ration, the Chief of Police,
having discovered that bad characters are transporting
foodstuffs of the city, has now issued strict orders
forbidding the export of foodstuffs from the city. It
is anticipated that there will be no more question about
foodstuffs.
Peking, Mar. 7th. After the second distribution of
foodstuffs here, most of the inhabitants have been unable
to purchase foodstuffs from the retail stores. The
supply is not enough to meet the demand. These stores
will cease to sell until the 27th instant. At the same
time, the police are making investigations to see if any
of the stores have eemmitted adulteration. Violators
will be severely punished.

Restrictions on Material Movements in Central China:
Nanking, Mar. 1lth. In September, 194l, the
authorities of the Japanese army and navy put in effect
"the Provisional Regulations Governing the Restrictions
on the Movements of Materials in Occupied Areas in the
Lower Yangtze Valley." Recently a new set of such
regulations has been decided upon in order to cope with
the present situation.
A similar action has been taken by the National
Government which has today decided upon "the Provisional
Restrictive Measures" during a session of the Supreme
Council for National Defence. The stipulations have
duly been published and made effective by both Japanese
and Chinese today.
Formerly it was necessary to restrict the movements
of materials with the object of intensifying the economic
blockade against the Chungking regime, especially in
Shanghai and certain other places where British and
American residents sided with the Chungking regime.
However, since the outbreak of the Greater Eastern
Asiatic War, the enemy's nationals have been unable to
display any great activity. For the purpose of increas-
ing the strength of the Chinese National Government, to
maintain the people's livelihood, and to win the good-
will of the people in order to facilitate the prosecution
of the war, it has now been decided to relax those
restriotions on the movements of materials in order that
materials may move freely and production may be inoreased.
During the session of the National Defence Council,
it has also been resolved to enforce "the Regulations
Governing the Establishment of the National Commeroial
Control General Commission" with the objeot of unifying
the purohase organs for materials in Central China.
However, movements of materials in areas adjaeent to enemy's
territory will still be striotly regulated.
Nanking, Mar. llth. On Maroh ll, the Minister of
Industries appointed 20 influential persons from financial
ciroles in Shanghai, including T'AnG Shou-min, etcetera,
to be the members of the National Commercial Control
General Commission. These members held a meeting in
Shanghai at 4 p.m. today.
Following are the views expressed by Japanese authori-
ties (Headquarters of the Japanese Army in Chine, Heae-
guarters of the Japanese Fleet in China, and the Japanese

=== Page 249 === (confidence 0.99)
-2-
The adjustment of the various commercial control
organs, which form the foundation of the basic
organization of the National Commercial Control
General Commission, will take considerable time.
Provisional measures, for the time being concerned
with the relaxation of the restrictions on material
movements in the Lower Yangtze Valley, have been
decided upon by the Japanese authorities and the
Chinese National Government after some consultation.
The following measures are effective as from March 16,
1943:
1. Prior to the establishment of the materials
collecting and distributing organization,
the restrictions on the movements of the
following materials in Shanghai and its
environs shall remain in force, while
movements of all the other materials shall
no longer be restricted:
The outward movement of cement, salt,
edible oils, woollen yarn, woollen textiles,
rayon, cloth, paper and tobacco.
The inward movement of rice (not including
glutinous rice), wheat, wheat flour, beans and
peas and cotton.
2。
The above-mentioned restrictions on movements
in Shanghai and its surroundings shall be
carried out by the Japanese and Chinese in
collaboration. It is decided that in the
nearest future they shall be abolished. The
permit service now enforced by the Japanese
army and navy shall also be discontinued and
thereafter such matters shall be handled by
the National Commercial Control General
Commission. However, permits previously issued
by the Japanese army and navy shall still have
effect within the period therein specified.
3. Restrictions on local movements shall be abolished
unless under special conditions. However, the
outflow of materials to enemy's territory shall
still be strictly banned.
The restrictions stipulated in the present
regulations shall be carried out by the Japanese
and Chinese authorities concerned. The Japanese
army shall not undertake such matters directly
unless deemed necessary from a military point
of view or in cases where the movements are in
localities adjacent to enemy's territory.
Manchuria to Increase Mineral Production:
Meisking, Mar. l3th. With the objeot of inereasing
the preduetien of war materials being supplied to Japan,
the Manehukuo Government has assigned the prinoipal mines
and rofimeries in the country the task of inereasing the

=== Page 250 === (confidence 0.99)
-3-
production of copper, lead and zino in the period from
April 1 to June 30. Production quotas are set for
the various mines and refineries with the hope of
increasing the efficiency, improving the technical
arts, bettering the utilization of materfals, and
preventing labor strikes, disasters, etcetera. At the
same time the Central Government with the cooperation
of the various organizations concerned is exerting
strenuous efforts towards the assurance of the supply
of materials and labor needed by the various mines and
the improvement of transportation facilities.
3.
Present Conditions in Sumatra:
Medan, Mar. 13th. Since the occupation of this
island a year ago, preparations have been made by the
military authorities for turning it into a strategic
base for the prosecution of the Greater Eastern Asiatic
War. Now this aim has been attained. Following are
the reports from various places reviewing the activities
during the past year:
1. Eastern Coastal Province. This province lies
in the northeast of Sumatra. It has an area about equal
to that of Taiwan (Formosa) and has a population of
149,000. This province has large-scale plantations of
rubber trees, palm (yielding palm oil), sesal hemp,
manila-hemp, tea, etcetera. It was the treasure of
Dutch East Indies. Of the 200-300 million guilders
which the Government of Dutch East Indies formerly
remitted to Holland, about half was derived from this
province. Prior to the outbreak of hostilities, the
annual production figures of its chief products were
as follows: rubber 360,000 tons, copra 215,000 tons
sesal hemp, manila-hemp, and other stiff fibers 58,000
tons, tea i,0oo tons and the well-noted tobacco of
Jih Li 25,000 tons. At the time when the Japanese Army
entered this province the factories of these plantations
had almost all been destroyed. Reconstruction of these
was first taken up. With regard to rubber trees, work
has been carried out by technical experts sent by the
Rubber Association at Singapore, restoring the planta-
tions owned by the Federal Farming Association of the
Eastern Coastal Province. The production there has
almost equaled the prewar level. At , in the north
of Sumatra work had been carried out Incessantly day
and night to raise sunken vessels and rebuild wharfs,
warehouses, etcetera, and complete restoration was
brought about in October l942. Bridges have been
repaired. The railroad has been prolonged by 564 km.
by the Jih Li Railway Company. Repeirs to 286 km. of
state-owned highway and 513 km. of established roads,
and restoration of radio and telephone services, have
been completed. 1t is planned to utilize the Tobd Lake
so establish a large eleotricity generating plant. At
present proparations are being steadily made for
establishing a large industrial area in the southern
part of this provinee.

=== Page 251 === (confidence 0.99)
2. Dabanuri (Tampat Towan ?). This province,
though not rich In mineral resources, has dense
forests which have never been cut. These forests
supply good building materials for ships. In aidition,
animal products are abundant, consisting of buffalo,
cattle, horses, sheep, hogs, etcetera. In the desert
island in the Toba Lake region, a limited number of
Merino sheep are found. It is planned to increase the
number of these sheep in the wide plain by the side of
the lake.
3. Achin. This province lies in the Northwestern
part of Sumatra. The population is 1,O00,O00. In the
south of this province kerosene oil is produced in
abundance. The production of rice is sufficient for
local requirements.
4。
Province. This province faces the
Indian Ocoan. It Is a large plain. Though in the
tropic zone, it has a good climate. Its population is
composed of the best tribes of the brown race. Both
industry and agriculture are important. The production
of rice is not only sufficient for the requirements of
the province but also leaves a surplus. It is well
known to the world for its production of quinine and
tea. Coal and coment are also produced.
5. Li Ao (Ringat ?). The population amounts to
480,000 and Is composed of native Malayans. A limited
quantity of rubber is usually produced here. Efforts
are being exerted towards the expansion of its rice
production and at the same time toward the production
of copra in the northern part of this province. It has
a rich deposit of coal. A large scale plan is in
formulation for opening the mines in Pa Ka Ba Erh
(Pakan Baroe ?).
6. Jambi. This province is for the most part
covered by forests.
7. Palembang. This province is for the most part
marshy. It has a population of about 1,300,000. It 1s
rich in kerosene oil. About 200 k.m. to the southwest
of the city of Palembang there are coal mines, the total
deposit of which amounts to about 900 million tons.
8. Lambang (Telok Betong ? ). This province lies
in the southernmost part of Sumatra and is very near

Present Conditions in Burma:
Rangoon, Mar. l7th. Economic reconstruction has
been carried out smoothly in Burma in spite of difficul-
ties. The latest economic conditions are as follows:
1. With regard to agriculture, a plan for attaining
self-sufficiency in foodstuffs is being carried out
step by step. At present rice and such products as
salt, sugar and edible oils, which usually had to be
imported, have attained a state of self-sufficiency.
Burma was originally rich in food production. The l94l-42
rice harvest was reported to be only a 50 per cent crop,
the decrease being attributed to fighting. However, a
survey now reveals that the crop was really around 70%
of normal. With regard to fish, it is difficult to have
fresh fish due to the hot weather in Burma. Orders have
therefore been issued to the fishery trade ordering them
to prepare large quantities of dried fish for the use of
the troops on the fronts.
2. Industrial manufactures for daily use are
generally self-sufficient. With regard to clothing,
home weaving is being encouraged. In addition, the
250,000 to 300,000 looms formerly used. are being put
into operation again. By June, idle equipment in Japan
will be made use of here. It is expected that the
production will even double the prewar level.
3. With regard to animal production, it is found
by the authorities after a survey that there are
altogether l0 million head of cattle. Leather is
already being manufactured. The number of horses is
sufficient for supplying the requirements of the South
Seas. Plans for propagation are being carried out.

The Grand Canal and Yellow River Projects:
Yangohow, Mar. l8th. The engineering work on the
repairing the section of the Grand Canal leading to
Yangohow will be completed in the course of a few days.
Peiping, Mar. 24th. Since the spring of 1938 whon
Generalissimo Chiang changed the flowing direction of
the Yellow River in the vicinity of Chengohow, the fields
lying in the Lower Yellow River Valley have felt a
shortage of water for irrigation purposes which has
hindered the expansion of agricultural production. For
the purpose of remedying the situation, the North China
Political Council's Planning Board decided some time ago
to take the following steps:
1. To build a large reservoir at Peiyangting, Taku,
Hopei Provinoe from whioh water may be let out through
the Ta Ch'ing River for irrigation purposes.
2. To conduot the water in the Yellow River into
the South Grand Canal.
The

=== Page 254 === (confidence 0.99)
-7-
The two above-mentioned great civil engineering
projects were to be carried out as soon as possible.
The first project was completed at the end or February
as originally fixed. The second project was to be
completed by the end of May. However, in order to
agree with the shipping plan for the whole of North
China, the volume of water to be conducted has had to
be increased. It has been decided to change the
original plan of conducting 25 cubic meters of water
per mow to 40 cubic meters per mow. For this reason,
the time limit has been extended to May of next year.
The revised plan is to conduct the water from the
vicinity of Chengchow in Honan Province to the South
Grand Canal in Shantung via Sinsiang in the northeast
and then the south part of Honan Province - a distance
of about 500 km. On the completion of this great
undertaking, it will contribute much toward the irriga-
tion of the North China plains. The North China
authorities have also decided to let out the stagnant
water in the muddy marshes near the Yungting River
between Tientsin and Yangtsun in order to irrigate the
fields in the vicinity of Tientsin.
Peking, Mar. 24th. Domei English News. It has
been disclosed that North China authorities are planning
to construct by May of next year a five-hundred kilometer
watercourse connecting the Yellow River with the Grand
Canal, to provide adequate irrigation for the paddy-
fields of the Tientsin area. The change in the course
of the Yellow River has caused subsidence in the flow
of the Hai River and the Grand Canal year after year,
with the result that the irrigation of the Tientsin area,
which is dependent upon these two sources, has become
difficult. The construction Bureau of the North China
Political Council therefore drew up plans to divert the
waters of the Yellow River into the Grand Canal and to
close the Poyang dam in order to discharge that water
into the Tatsing River. The work on closing the Poyang
dam was completed at the end of February this year,
according to plan, while the diversion of the waters
of the Yellow River is planned for spring of next year.
The projected undertaking, constructing a five-hundred
kilometer waterway from a point north of Chengohow,
Honan Province, to the Grand Canal via Hsinsiang, Honan
Province, is expected to take six million man-days of
labor. The water from the Yellow River will add to the
transportation facilities of North China.
